## Answer Key: Chapter 5 {#sec-solutions-ch5 .unnumbered}

Full solutions to Chapter 5's "Check your understanding" questions
(@sec-ch5-check).

**1. Conceptual distinction. A colleague reports "peak memory: 42 GiB"
for a training run without saying more. List the five kinds of memory
number this chapter distinguishes, and state which one a bare "peak
memory" figure from `nvidia-smi` actually is — and why it might not
even be a true peak.**

*Answer.* The five kinds are: logical tensor memory (the exact byte
count a tensor's shape and dtype imply); an analytical/theoretical
estimate (a formula applied to a configuration — either an idealized
lower bound under a stated sharding/recomputation policy, or a direct
estimate, computed in advance); a framework max-allocated counter
(e.g. PyTorch's `max_memory_allocated`, a running maximum the
framework itself tracks); a framework max-reserved/allocator-level
counter (e.g. `max_memory_reserved`, which additionally includes
allocator fragmentation and reserved-but-unused blocks); and sampled
device framebuffer usage via `nvidia-smi` or similar — a point-in-time
external observation. A bare `nvidia-smi` figure is the fifth kind,
and it is only a genuine *peak* if the sampling procedure itself
tracked a running maximum; a single query, or one polled too loosely,
can report a value well below the run's real peak without any
indication that it did so.

*Common trap:* Assuming any `nvidia-smi` reading is automatically the
run's true peak, or treating a measured/sampled number as if it were a
clean logical/theoretical count — the two can differ because sampled
and allocator-level memory include fragmentation, framework overhead,
and sampling-instant luck that a formula-based estimate does not
model.

**2. Calculation. A model has N=2 billion parameters, trained in mixed
precision. What is the per-rank model-state memory (a) under vanilla
data parallelism, and (b) under ZeRO-3 with a data-parallel degree of
4?**

*Answer.* (a) Vanilla DP: $16N = 16 \times 2\times10^9 = 3.2\times10^{10}$
bytes $\approx 29.8$ GiB, fully replicated on every rank. (b) ZeRO-3
with $N_d=4$: $16N/4 \approx 7.45$ GiB per rank — the same four objects
(bf16 params, bf16 gradients, fp32 master weights, fp32 Adam state),
each divided by 4.

*Common trap:* Forgetting that mixed precision's total is still $16N$
(not $8N$ or some other "halved" value) before any sharding is
applied — see this chapter's own common-misconception callout.

**3. Calculation. For a model with hidden size h=4096 and a
data-parallel degree of 16, using this chapter's declared convention
(one-direction send volume per rank for a ring all-gather, not local
shard size), how many MiB does one rank SEND during one ZeRO-3
forward-pass all-gather of a single transformer block's parameters
(bf16)?**

*Answer.* The full block tensor has $16h^2 = 16 \times 4096^2 =
268{,}435{,}456$ elements; in bf16, $536{,}870{,}912$ bytes $=512$ MiB.
The local shard — what one rank *stores*, not what it *communicates*
— is $512/16=32$ MiB. The ring all-gather send volume per rank is
$\frac{N_d-1}{N_d}\times512 = \frac{15}{16}\times512=480$ MiB; the
receive volume per rank is the same, $480$ MiB, by ring symmetry.

*Common trap:* Reporting the local shard size (32 MiB) as if it were
the communication payload — the exact bug an earlier draft of this
chapter's own worked example made and then corrected — or reporting
the element count as if it were already a byte count.

**4. Bottleneck diagnosis. A training job's per-GPU throughput drops
as more GPUs are added to a fixed-size problem, and profiling shows
idle time between layers while waiting for parameter transfers to
finish. Which resource most plausibly bounds this step, and which
quantity from this chapter would you check first to confirm it?**

*Answer.* The symptom (idle time waiting specifically for parameter
transfers, worsening as more GPUs are added to the same problem size)
points to an interconnect-bandwidth bottleneck, not a compute
bottleneck — this is exactly the pattern Megatron-LM's own scaling
experiment reports once "the per-GPU computation decreases and the
memory bandwidth and communication overheads begin to dominate." The
first thing to check is the relevant overlap ratio
($t_{\text{comm}}/t_{\text{compute}}$) for whichever strategy is
sharding/communicating parameters — if that ratio exceeds 1, the
communication cannot be fully hidden and will show up as exactly this
kind of idle time.

*Common trap:* Assuming more GPUs always means more throughput, or
blaming compute (e.g. recommending a bigger batch size) without first
checking whether the bottleneck is actually bandwidth.

**5. Synthesis/design. A 2-billion-parameter model (mixed precision)
is trained with ZeRO-3 sharding of its model-state memory across the
data-parallel group, combined with ideal, even tensor-parallel
partitioning, on a cluster whose total world size is fixed at 24
devices split only between DP and TP (no PP, CP, or EP). A 10
GiB-per-device memory budget is declared. (a) Write per-device
model-state memory as a function of DP and TP under this combination,
and show that for every valid factorization of $DP\times TP=24$ (e.g.
DP=3/TP=8, DP=4/TP=6, DP=6/TP=4, DP=8/TP=3), the budget is satisfied by
the same margin — i.e. the memory budget alone cannot select a unique
(DP, TP) split. (b) Name one additional constraint or measured
quantity that would pin down a unique split, and explain concretely
how it breaks the tie.**

*Answer.* (a) Under combined ZeRO-3 DP sharding and even TP
partitioning, both axes shard the same model-state objects, so
per-device model-state memory is $16N/(DP\times TP)$. Because the
world size fixes $DP\times TP=24$, this is $16N/24$ for *every* valid
factorization — substituting $N=2\times10^9$ gives
$16\times2\times10^9/24\approx1.24$ GiB/device, regardless of whether
$(DP,TP)$ is $(3,8)$, $(4,6)$, $(6,4)$, $(8,3)$, $(12,2)$, or $(24,1)$.
Every one of these factorizations fits the 10 GiB budget by the
identical $\approx8.76$ GiB margin, so the budget inequality
$16N/(DP\times TP)\le10\text{ GiB}$ is satisfied the same way no
matter how the 24 devices are split between the two axes — the memory
budget contains no information that could favor one split over
another. (b) Any one concrete, correctly justified constraint breaks
the tie: TP must evenly divide the model's attention/KV head count,
which bounds which TP values are even feasible (e.g. 8 KV heads rules
out TP=12 or TP=24); the global batch size must be evenly divisible by
DP; the TP activation all-gather's communication cost (this chapter's
overlap ratio, which depends only on $h$ and the TP degree) trades off
against DP's memory benefit, so two memory-equivalent splits are not
equally fast; per-layer temporary/workspace memory (outside the $16N$
model-state formula) can scale differently with TP than with DP;
network topology (TP needs fast intra-node bandwidth, bounding TP by
node size); or measured per-configuration throughput from real runs.
Any of these — not the memory budget — is what would actually select
one factorization over another.

*Common trap:* Computing per-device memory as $16N/DP$ alone, ignoring
that even TP partitioning *also* shards model-state memory — this
wrongly suggests a "minimum DP" exists on memory grounds alone, when
in fact $DP\times TP=24$ is fixed and $16N/(DP\times TP)$ never
changes across factorizations. (An earlier version of this question
used exactly that flawed $16N/DP$-only framing and concluded DP=3 was
uniquely forced; that conclusion does not survive once TP's own
sharding contribution is correctly accounted for, and is not the
answer here.)
